questions.passage: [i]A Burial at Ornans[/i], painted in the realist style by Gustave Courbet, depicts an ordinary provincial funeral in stark detail. The realists’ emphasis on accurately portraying the experiences of average working people was largely a rejection of the romantic style evident in many paintings by Isidore Pils, which instead [vocab]______[/vocab] their subjects’ positive traits, altering subjects to appear more beautiful or heroic than they actually were.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: apprehend

choices.label: B
choices.text: magnify

choices.label: C
choices.text: rectify

choices.label: D
choices.text: counteract

explanation.short: The paintings make favorable qualities look larger than they really are, so “magnify” supplies the exact contrast with realist accuracy.
explanation.key_evidence: Pils’s subjects are altered to appear “more beautiful or heroic than they actually were.”
explanation.why_correct: The sentence describes deliberate idealization: the paintings enlarge already positive traits beyond reality. “Magnify” names that enlargement and preserves the contrast with accurate realist portrayal.
explanation.detailed: Realism is defined here by fidelity to ordinary experience, whereas Pils’s romantic style beautifies or heroizes its subjects. A verb meaning “make seem greater” is required, and only “magnify” expresses that operation.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“apprehend”): Incorrect—“Apprehend” means understand, perceive, or arrest; the paintings are not grasping the traits but exaggerating them.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“magnify”): Correct—“Magnify” means make something seem greater, exactly matching the stated beautification and heroization.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“rectify”): Incorrect—“Rectify” means correct an error; the text says the images depart from reality rather than correct it.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“counteract”): Incorrect—“Counteract” means act against an effect, which reverses the idea that romantic paintings heighten favorable traits.

questions.passage: Quinoa grain was domesticated in South America. Its physical structure is no longer identical to the structure of the wild plant it is descended from. Maize (corn) also [vocab]______[/vocab] its wild ancestor. That ancestor plant had a few small kernels. Indigenous people in Mexico carefully bred the crop until it had numerous fleshy kernels.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: helps with

choices.label: B
choices.text: varies from

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues with

choices.label: D
choices.text: reacts to

explanation.short: Selective breeding changed maize from an ancestor with a few small kernels to a crop with many fleshy ones, so modern maize “varies from” that ancestor.
explanation.key_evidence: The wild ancestor had a few small kernels; Indigenous breeding produced numerous fleshy kernels.
explanation.why_correct: The sentence asks for the relationship between present maize and its wild ancestor. The described structural changes establish difference, making “varies from” the only semantically accurate phrase.
explanation.detailed: The quinoa example establishes a pattern of domesticated crops no longer being physically identical to their ancestors. The maize details then demonstrate the same pattern through kernel number and size.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“helps with”): Incorrect—“Helps with” would imply that maize assists its ancestor, an unsupported relationship between a crop and an ancestral plant.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“varies from”): Correct—“Varies from” directly states the physical difference demonstrated by the contrast in kernel size and number.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“argues with”): Incorrect—“Argues with” personifies the plants and introduces a dispute that the passage never describes.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“reacts to”): Incorrect—“Reacts to” would require an action or stimulus from the ancestor; the text instead compares two structures.

questions.passage: The collectibles market is one of the most difficult segments of the consumer economy to [vocab]______[/vocab]. Few economists would have predicted, for example, that the prices of vintage movie posters would soar in the 2010s, but soar they did.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: forecast

choices.label: B
choices.text: monitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: avoid

choices.label: D
choices.text: exchange

explanation.short: The unexpected surge in vintage-poster prices illustrates how hard the collectibles market is to forecast.
explanation.key_evidence: Few economists predicted that vintage movie-poster prices would soar in the 2010s.
explanation.why_correct: The example in the passage concerns a future price movement that experts failed to anticipate. Since “forecast” means predict in advance, it connects the general claim to the poster-price example precisely.
explanation.detailed: The second sentence is evidence for the first: economists did not foresee a major market change. That evidence identifies prediction—not observation, avoidance, or trade—as the difficult activity.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“forecast”): Correct—“Forecast” names advance prediction, exactly the task economists failed to perform in the example.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“monitor”): Incorrect—“Monitor” means track an ongoing market; economists could observe prices even if they could not predict the later surge.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“avoid”): Incorrect—“Avoid” concerns staying away from the market, which is irrelevant to the surprise about future prices.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“exchange”): Incorrect—“Exchange” means trade one thing for another and does not describe estimating how prices will change.

questions.passage: Tsuruoka, Japan, was named a City of Gastronomy by UNESCO in 2014, a title that [vocab]______[/vocab] that Tsuruoka has a unique and vibrant food culture worthy of celebration.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: complains

choices.label: B
choices.text: denotes

choices.label: C
choices.text: discovers

choices.label: D
choices.text: renounces

explanation.short: The UNESCO designation signifies a recognized quality of Tsuruoka, so the title “denotes” its distinctive food culture.
explanation.key_evidence: The title is followed by the proposition that Tsuruoka has a food culture worthy of celebration.
explanation.why_correct: The relative clause explains what the title signifies about the city. “Denotes” means indicates or represents, so it correctly links the designation to the quality it recognizes.
explanation.detailed: A formal title does not perform an action toward the city; it carries meaning. Here that meaning is UNESCO recognition of Tsuruoka’s unique and vibrant food culture.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“complains”): Incorrect—“Complains” requires an expression of dissatisfaction, which neither the title nor UNESCO’s recognition supplies.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“denotes”): Correct—“Denotes” accurately means that the title indicates Tsuruoka’s recognized gastronomic status.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“discovers”): Incorrect—“Discovers” would make the title an investigator and misstates recognition as the act of finding something new.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“renounces”): Incorrect—“Renounces” means gives up or rejects, the opposite of a title celebrating Tsuruoka’s food culture.

questions.passage: The following text is from Louise Erdrich’s 1986 novel [i]The Beet Queen[/i]. Celestine takes her infant daughter with her to the butcher shop where she makes sausages. Sometimes Celestine turned around and met the direct gaze of her daughter, a look so penetrating that Celestine’s breath caught. She dropped the spice, the string, the knife she was using, and took the girl up in her arms, ready for her to speak as if a spell had suddenly lifted. When the baby flexed her entire body and struggled to free herself, Celestine put her down. No matter how thorough Celestine’s exhaustion, no matter how little sleep she’d had, there was a nerve of excitement running through each hour. ©1986 by Louise Erdrich
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To demonstrate Celestine’s unhappiness in the workplace

choices.label: B
choices.text: To portray Celestine’s excitement about her daughter

choices.label: C
choices.text: To show that Celestine enjoys imagining her daughter’s future life

choices.label: D
choices.text: To consider how Celestine’s coworkers feel about her daughter

explanation.short: The scene portrays Celestine’s intense excitement about her infant daughter even through physical exhaustion.
explanation.key_evidence: Celestine stops working to lift the baby and feels “a nerve of excitement” despite little sleep.
explanation.why_correct: The text repeatedly centers Celestine’s heightened response to her daughter: the baby’s gaze catches her breath, interrupts her work, and sustains excitement through fatigue. That pattern establishes the stated purpose.
explanation.detailed: Every narrated action belongs to the mother-daughter interaction, culminating in the explicit description of excitement. The passage is therefore a portrait of Celestine’s emotional absorption in her daughter, not a workplace complaint or prediction of the child’s future.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“To demonstrate Celestine’s unhappiness in the workplace”): Incorrect—Workplace unhappiness is unsupported: the dropped tools result from the baby’s penetrating gaze, and exhaustion comes from little sleep, not dissatisfaction with sausage making.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“To portray Celestine’s excitement about her daughter”): Correct—The baby’s gaze, Celestine’s impulse to hold her, and the explicit “nerve of excitement” all support this purpose.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“To show that Celestine enjoys imagining her daughter’s future life”): Incorrect—Celestine briefly expects the baby to speak, but the text does not develop imagined future events or say she enjoys envisioning the daughter’s later life.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“To consider how Celestine’s coworkers feel about her daughter”): Incorrect—No coworkers appear or express any reaction, so their feelings cannot be the passage’s purpose.

questions.passage:
校订说明：编辑校订：依据美国国会图书馆与 NABJ 的一手资料，修正报纸创办者姓名及相应指代，并准确表述 NABJ 的支持与倡议职能。此为来源事实勘误，不是官方题面复原。

In 1827, Samuel E. Cornish and John Brown Russwurm, supported by other leading free Black men in New York City, founded [i]Freedom’s Journal[/i], America’s first Black-owned-and-operated newspaper. Their accomplishment is just one example of the rich history of Black journalism in the United States. The National Association of Black Journalists, founded in Washington, DC, in 1975, supports Black media professionals and recognizes the achievements of Black journalists, helping to uphold that history.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It introduces the history of an organization honoring Black journalists, then suggests how that organization might recruit more members.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It mentions a specific achievement in Black journalistic history, then describes an organization dedicated to upholding that history.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It summarizes a theory about journalism, then explains how a journalistic practice has changed over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It describes the career of a well-known figure in Black journalism, then compares that career to one of a figure who is lesser known.

explanation.short: The passage moves from a landmark newspaper's founding to an organization supporting Black journalism.
explanation.key_evidence: The first sentence presents Freedom’s Journal; the last describes the National Association of Black Journalists.
explanation.why_correct: B captures both parts in their actual order: a particular historical achievement followed by an organization that upholds the wider journalistic tradition.
explanation.detailed: The opening example is concrete: Cornish and Russwurm founded a pioneering newspaper in 1827. The middle sentence places that achievement within the broader history of Black journalism. The final sentence then introduces NABJ and its continuing support for Black journalists. This is an example-to-institution progression, not a recruitment proposal, a theory of journalism or a comparison between two individual careers.

choice_analysis.A: The text does not suggest recruiting methods, and its first topic is a newspaper's founding rather than the organization's own history.
choice_analysis.B: The 1827 founding is a specific historical achievement; the later description of NABJ explains how an organization upholds the broader tradition.
choice_analysis.C: No theory or changing journalistic practice is presented. Two historical dates alone do not establish the structure this choice describes.
choice_analysis.D: Cornish and Russwurm's accomplishment is not compared with a lesser-known person's career; the later subject is an association.

questions.passage: Though Vasily Grossman’s novel [i]Stalingrad[/i] is considered inferior to his later work [i]Life and Fate[/i], some critics praise it despite an arduous writing process required to satisfy Soviet censors (Marcel Theroux in [i]The Guardian[/i] called [i]Stalingrad[/i] “lucid and readable”). Of the novel’s eleven drafts, the first is largely illegible, the sixth closely hews to Soviet orthodoxy, and published versions most resemble the fifth. The English edition’s translators culled material from unpublished drafts and published Russian versions to create a comprehensive edition.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It refers to a novel that has several different published and unpublished versions, identifies characteristics that have led critics to prefer one version to others, and tells how translators justified their choice to bring one particular version of the novel into another language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It mentions a novel whose quality critics do not agree on, discusses obstacles that make it difficult to determine what the best version of that novel might be, and offers a reason why some critics find a translation of the novel to be superior to the original.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It describes a novel whose critical reputation has declined over time, explains the cause of that decline, and reports the effort of translators to rehabilitate a work they believe has been unjustly ignored.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It notes a novel’s critical reception, addresses the complicated history of the novel’s development, and suggests how that history informed the work of the novel’s English translators.

explanation.short: The text progresses from Stalingrad’s mixed reception, through its censorship-shaped draft history, to the translators’ use of that history in constructing the English edition.
explanation.key_evidence: Reception appears first; eleven drafts and Soviet censorship follow; the final sentence explains the translators’ composite edition.
explanation.why_correct: Each part of choice D maps to a distinct passage segment. The critical judgment frames the novel, the draft evidence shows complicated development, and the translators’ selection from several versions shows how that development informed their work.
explanation.detailed: The passage does not choose one authoritative draft. Instead, it explains why the textual history is complex and how the English translators responded by combining unpublished drafts with published Russian versions.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“It refers to a novel that has several different published and unpublished versions, identifies characteristics that have led critics to prefer one version to others, and tells how translators justified their choice to bring one particular version of the novel into another language.”): Incorrect—The passage never says critics prefer one particular version or that the translators brought only that version into English; they culled from several sources.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“It mentions a novel whose quality critics do not agree on, discusses obstacles that make it difficult to determine what the best version of that novel might be, and offers a reason why some critics find a translation of the novel to be superior to the original.”): Incorrect—It does not report disagreement among critics about the best draft or claim that critics consider the translation superior to the original.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“It describes a novel whose critical reputation has declined over time, explains the cause of that decline, and reports the effort of translators to rehabilitate a work they believe has been unjustly ignored.”): Incorrect—No decline in reputation over time is described, and the translators are not presented as rehabilitating an ignored work.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“It notes a novel’s critical reception, addresses the complicated history of the novel’s development, and suggests how that history informed the work of the novel’s English translators.”): Correct—Critical reception, complicated development across drafts, and the translators’ composite method are the passage’s actual three stages.

questions.passage: Hydroelectric generators and many other widely used mechanical systems have moving parts that rub or slide against one another, creating friction. This friction increases energy consumption and causes wear, which decreases the stability and life span of the system. Using carbon nanotubes and oil, Chanaka Kumara and colleagues at a US Department of Energy lab have created a coating for moving parts that reduces friction to the point where it is almost nonexistent. The new coating is suitable for common applications, unlike other approaches that require special conditions.
questions.prompt: What does the text most strongly suggest about the coating created by Kumara and colleagues?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is unlikely to be widely used because it can be applied only under special conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can likely improve the energy consumption of certain mechanical systems but not of hydroelectric generators.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is unlikely to reduce wear in mechanical systems that have multiple moving parts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It can likely be used to reduce energy consumption and wear in hydroelectric generators and other common mechanical systems.

explanation.short: A near-frictionless coating usable in ordinary settings could lower both energy loss and mechanical wear in hydroelectric generators and similar machines.
explanation.key_evidence: Friction raises energy consumption and wear; the new coating nearly eliminates friction and suits common applications.
explanation.why_correct: The passage identifies two harms caused by friction, then says the coating removes almost all friction without requiring special conditions. Applying that cause-and-effect chain supports benefits for the named generator systems and other common machinery.
explanation.detailed: Hydroelectric generators are introduced as an example of systems with rubbing parts. Since the coating addresses the shared source of wasted energy and wear and is suitable for normal use, the inference properly includes those generators rather than excluding them.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“It is unlikely to be widely used because it can be applied only under special conditions.”): Incorrect—This reverses the final sentence: special conditions limit other approaches, while Kumara’s coating is suitable for common applications.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“It can likely improve the energy consumption of certain mechanical systems but not of hydroelectric generators.”): Incorrect—The passage explicitly includes hydroelectric generators among friction-affected systems, so excluding them is unsupported.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“It is unlikely to reduce wear in mechanical systems that have multiple moving parts.”): Incorrect—Reducing friction should reduce the wear friction causes; the number of moving parts is never given as a limitation.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“It can likely be used to reduce energy consumption and wear in hydroelectric generators and other common mechanical systems.”): Correct—This choice follows both stated effects of friction and the coating’s stated suitability for common mechanical applications.

questions.passage: Optimal foraging theory (OFT) holds that animals’ foraging behaviors reflect cost-benefit trade-offs that vary by species and with dynamic ecological circumstances. One such circumstance is lunar intensity, which Paul C. Griffiths and colleagues found to be negatively associated with foraging by snowshoe hares but Ian C. Colquhoun found to be positively associated with foraging by black lemurs. This discrepancy is explicable in terms of OFT: the lemurs’ greater reliance on vision means that higher lunar intensity benefits them more than it benefits the hares.
questions.prompt: Information in the text best supports which statement about OFT?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can explain why some species act in accordance with cost-benefit trade-offs and others do not.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It may be weakened by the finding that the costs and benefits associated with a particular ecological circumstance vary by species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It tends to allow for a better understanding of the benefits of ecological circumstances than the costs of those circumstances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It can account for observations of different species responding differently to similar ecological circumstances.

explanation.short: OFT explains the hare and lemur’s opposite responses to moonlight by assigning different species-specific benefits to the same circumstance.
explanation.key_evidence: Moonlight decreases hare foraging but increases lemur foraging; lemurs’ greater visual reliance gives them more benefit.
explanation.why_correct: The text treats both behaviors as cost-benefit responses under OFT. Species differ in how useful lunar light is, so the theory can account for different reactions to the same ecological condition.
explanation.detailed: The apparent discrepancy is not a failure of OFT: its premise already allows trade-offs to vary by species and circumstance. Greater visual reliance changes the benefit side for lemurs, resolving the contrast with hares.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“It can explain why some species act in accordance with cost-benefit trade-offs and others do not.”): Incorrect—The text does not divide species into those following trade-offs and those ignoring them; both examples are explained through trade-offs.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“It may be weakened by the finding that the costs and benefits associated with a particular ecological circumstance vary by species.”): Incorrect—Species-specific costs and benefits are built into OFT and explain the finding, so the variation strengthens this application rather than weakening it.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“It tends to allow for a better understanding of the benefits of ecological circumstances than the costs of those circumstances.”): Incorrect—The passage compares differing benefits but never claims that OFT generally explains benefits better than costs.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“It can account for observations of different species responding differently to similar ecological circumstances.”): Correct—This accurately summarizes how one theory accommodates the contrasting hare and lemur observations.

questions.passage: High-speed rail (HSR) systems have trains that move at much higher speeds than traditional trains. HSR is expanding in Switzerland, Uzbekistan, and many other countries around the world. The United States, however, has been slow to build HSR systems. Researchers surveyed United States residents about their attitudes toward HSR. [u]The researchers claim that this survey reveals that there is strong support for building more HSR lines in the United States.[/u]
questions.prompt: Which quotation from a survey respondent would best illustrate the underlined claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: “I prefer riding buses instead of taking trains because buses travel to more locations.”

choices.label: B
choices.text: “I have traveled on high-speed rail lines in Switzerland but not in Uzbekistan.”

choices.label: C
choices.text: “I think high-speed rail is wonderful. The United States needs to build more high-speed rail lines.”

choices.label: D
choices.text: “I believe that the United States has enough high-speed rail lines. It should invest in airports instead.”

explanation.short: The respondent who calls HSR wonderful and explicitly asks the United States to build more lines directly illustrates strong support.
explanation.key_evidence: The underlined claim concerns support for constructing additional US high-speed rail lines.
explanation.why_correct: The text of choice C provides both a strongly favorable evaluation and an unambiguous recommendation for more US lines. Those two statements directly instantiate the researchers’ claim about strong public support.
explanation.detailed: To illustrate the claim, a quotation must endorse HSR expansion in the United States. Merely discussing travel experience or other transportation does not show that position, while opposition would contradict it.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (““I prefer riding buses instead of taking trains because buses travel to more locations.””): Incorrect—Preferring buses to trains expresses a competing transportation preference and offers no support for adding HSR lines.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (““I have traveled on high-speed rail lines in Switzerland but not in Uzbekistan.””): Incorrect—Travel in Switzerland but not Uzbekistan reports personal experience without stating any view on US construction.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (““I think high-speed rail is wonderful. The United States needs to build more high-speed rail lines.””): Correct—Calling HSR “wonderful” and saying the United States “needs to build more” supplies the exact attitude claimed.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (““I believe that the United States has enough high-speed rail lines. It should invest in airports instead.””): Incorrect—Saying the United States has enough lines and should fund airports directly contradicts expansion.

questions.passage: Elisabeth Pötzelsberger and colleagues gathered data on 23 non-native tree species grown in Europe. They analyzed reports from Italy, Denmark, and Belgium about the number of these species grown in those countries as well as the numbers of insect and fungus species that damage those trees. The researchers concluded that Italy had a greater number of damaging fungus species than either of the other countries did.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Pötzelsberger and colleagues’ conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Belgium reported 13 damaging fungus species but only 11 damaging insect species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Italy reported 57 damaging fungus species, whereas Denmark reported 33 damaging insect species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Italy reported 57 damaging fungus species, which is more than either Denmark or Belgium reported.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Denmark and Belgium reported 12 and 4 damaging fungus species, respectively, which is far fewer than Italy reported.

explanation.short: Italy’s 57 damaging fungus species exceeds the fungus totals for both Denmark and Belgium, directly supporting the researchers’ comparison.
explanation.key_evidence: The table lists fungus totals of 57 for Italy, 22 for Denmark, and 13 for Belgium.
explanation.why_correct: The conclusion compares one variable—damaging fungus species—across three countries. Choice C preserves that variable and correctly states that Italy’s 57 is greater than each of the other two totals.
explanation.detailed: Evidence must compare Italy with both Denmark and Belgium using fungus counts. Cross-category comparisons with insects or incorrect table values cannot establish the stated ranking.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Belgium reported 13 damaging fungus species but only 11 damaging insect species.”): Incorrect—Belgium’s fungus-versus-insect comparison says nothing about whether Italy has more fungus species than Belgium and Denmark.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Italy reported 57 damaging fungus species, whereas Denmark reported 33 damaging insect species.”): Incorrect—This compares Italy’s fungus count with Denmark’s insect count, mixing variables and omitting Belgium.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Italy reported 57 damaging fungus species, which is more than either Denmark or Belgium reported.”): Correct—The statement accurately reports Italy’s 57 as higher than both Denmark’s 22 and Belgium’s 13.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Denmark and Belgium reported 12 and 4 damaging fungus species, respectively, which is far fewer than Italy reported.”): Incorrect—The claimed Denmark and Belgium fungus values, 12 and 4, misreport the table’s 22 and 13.

questions.passage: [i]Life Among the Paiutes[/i] is an 1882 autobiographical narrative by Sarah Winnemucca Hopkins. In the work, Winnemucca explicitly indicates when and how she is shifting the focus of the narrative, as when she writes, ______
questions.prompt: Which quotation from [i]Life Among the Paiutes[/i] most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: “I will now stop writing about myself and family and tribe customs, and tell about the wars, and the causes of the wars. I will jump over about six years.”

choices.label: B
choices.text: “Now, my dear reader, there is no word so endearing as the word father, and that is why [my people] call all good people father or mother.”

choices.label: C
choices.text: “But how can I describe the scene that followed? Some of you, dear readers, can imagine.”

choices.label: D
choices.text: “During the time my grandfather was away in California, where he [stayed] till after the Mexican war, there was a girl-baby born in our family.”

explanation.short: The first quotation explicitly announces both a topic change and a six-year jump in the narrative.
explanation.key_evidence: “I will now stop writing about myself ... and tell about the wars ... I will jump over about six years.”
explanation.why_correct: The claim requires the narrator to signal when and how focus changes. Choice A does both by naming the abandoned and new subjects and stating the span of time skipped.
explanation.detailed: Only the first quotation contains metanarrative directions about organization: it marks a transition from personal, family, and tribal customs to wars and their causes and identifies a chronological leap.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (““I will now stop writing about myself and family and tribe customs, and tell about the wars, and the causes of the wars. I will jump over about six years.””): Correct—This is the exact organizational signal described: it identifies the old topic, new topic, and time jump.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (““Now, my dear reader, there is no word so endearing as the word father, and that is why [my people] call all good people father or mother.””): Incorrect—Addressing the reader while explaining the word “father” continues a topic; it does not announce a shift in narrative focus.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (““But how can I describe the scene that followed? Some of you, dear readers, can imagine.””): Incorrect—The rhetorical question concerns difficulty describing a scene, not a change of subject or chronology.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (““During the time my grandfather was away in California, where he [stayed] till after the Mexican war, there was a girl-baby born in our family.””): Incorrect—The sentence narrates a birth during the grandfather’s absence but does not explicitly mark how the narrative is being reorganized.

questions.passage: Studies have found that when looking at other people’s eyes, humans tend to perceive dilated pupils positively and constricted pupils negatively. Noting that a dark iris—the colored portion surrounding the pupil—is hard to distinguish from the black of the pupil (and thereby affects the pupil’s apparent size) and that many domestic dogs have dark irises, Akitsugu Konno et al. showed close-up images of dogs’ faces to human participants and asked them to rate the dogs’ traits and their own attitudes toward the dogs. Their findings suggest that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: humans’ responses to pupil size in other people may extend to dogs, as participants responded more positively to images of dogs whose iris colors were likely to make their pupils appear large than they did to images of dogs whose iris colors were unlikely to have that effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: differences in dogs’ pupil size may elicit a stronger response in humans than differences in people’s pupil size do, as participants’ responses to the images when dogs’ pupils were actually large were indistinguishable from participants’ responses when dogs’ pupils only appeared to be large due to iris color.

choices.label: C
choices.text: iris color in domestic dogs may be an adaptation to elicit positive responses from humans, as participants responded more negatively to images of dogs whose iris colors can make pupils appear large than they did to images of dogs without such iris colors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: humans may not be as sensitive to pupil size in dogs as they are to pupil size in other people, as participants’ responses to the images show no relationship to differences in the shade of dogs’ irises that could affect how large the dogs’ pupils appear to be.

explanation.short: Participants rated dark-irised dogs more positively, consistent with the idea that irises making pupils appear larger elicit the favorable response seen with human pupils.
explanation.key_evidence: Dark irises blend with pupils and enlarge their apparent size; the table shows more positive ratings for the dark-iris images.
explanation.why_correct: The passage’s study manipulates an iris feature that changes apparent pupil size. The more favorable ratings for dogs with dark irises extend the established human response to apparently dilated pupils to dogs.
explanation.detailed: The inference is limited to the observed association: iris shade can make a dog’s pupil look larger, and participants’ trait and attitude ratings shift positively in that condition. It does not establish evolution, actual pupil dilation, or a stronger effect than in humans.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“humans’ responses to pupil size in other people may extend to dogs, as participants responded more positively to images of dogs whose iris colors were likely to make their pupils appear large than they did to images of dogs whose iris colors were unlikely to have that effect.”): Correct—This accurately links the dark-iris condition, larger apparent pupils, and the table’s more positive participant responses.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“differences in dogs’ pupil size may elicit a stronger response in humans than differences in people’s pupil size do, as participants’ responses to the images when dogs’ pupils were actually large were indistinguishable from participants’ responses when dogs’ pupils only appeared to be large due to iris color.”): Incorrect—The study compares iris colors that alter apparent size, not actual large pupils versus merely apparent large pupils, and supplies no human-dog effect-size comparison.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“iris color in domestic dogs may be an adaptation to elicit positive responses from humans, as participants responded more negatively to images of dogs whose iris colors can make pupils appear large than they did to images of dogs without such iris colors.”): Incorrect—The direction is reversed: participants responded more positively, not more negatively, to the iris condition associated with larger-looking pupils; adaptation is also unsupported.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“humans may not be as sensitive to pupil size in dogs as they are to pupil size in other people, as participants’ responses to the images show no relationship to differences in the shade of dogs’ irises that could affect how large the dogs’ pupils appear to be.”): Incorrect—The table does show a relationship between iris shade and ratings, so claiming no sensitivity contradicts the reported pattern.

questions.passage: Across brown bears—omnivores with high dietary plasticity—there is wide variety in dietary mix, which may reflect genetics, local resource availability, or social learning (cubs stay with their mothers for two years or more). Evaluating these possibilities, Anne Hertel et al. analyzed 30 years of data on trophic position (indicative of dietary mix) for female brown bears. After separation, daughters, who tended to settle near their mothers, occupied the same trophic positions as their mothers for two years, but the correlation disappeared by year five. Trophic correlation with unrelated individuals in similar habitats was modest, while habitat-independent correlation with nonmaternal relatives (e.g., cousins) was no different than with unrelated individuals. These findings suggest that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: social learning and resource fluctuations may both play a role in dietary mix among females, at least temporarily, though genetic factors appear to make a significant contribution as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: growing dissimilarity between mothers and their daughters with regard to dietary mix may reflect changes in the resources available in maternal habitats, though social learning could also contribute to the trend.

choices.label: C
choices.text: female dietary mix is best understood as changeable and contingent on fluctuating environmental conditions rather than as the result of social learning or genetic factors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: dietary mix among females may reflect a social learning effect that eventually diminishes, though environmental constraints cannot be ruled out as a contributing factor.

explanation.short: The temporary mother-daughter match points to fading social learning, while modest habitat similarity leaves environmental constraints possible and the relative data do not support genetics.
explanation.key_evidence: Mother-daughter trophic correlation vanishes by year five; nonmaternal relatives resemble unrelated bears, while habitat peers show modest correlation.
explanation.why_correct: The passage’s two-year-to-five-year pattern fits a learned maternal diet that persists briefly after separation and then weakens. The habitat correlation preserves an environmental explanation, whereas the lack of extra similarity among relatives argues against a genetic contribution.
explanation.detailed: The three comparisons separate candidate causes. The time-limited maternal link fits social transmission; some resemblance among bears in similar habitats fits resources; and cousins performing no better than unrelated bears provides no positive genetic signal.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“social learning and resource fluctuations may both play a role in dietary mix among females, at least temporarily, though genetic factors appear to make a significant contribution as well.”): Incorrect—The claim of a significant genetic contribution conflicts with the finding that nonmaternal relatives are no more correlated than unrelated bears.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“growing dissimilarity between mothers and their daughters with regard to dietary mix may reflect changes in the resources available in maternal habitats, though social learning could also contribute to the trend.”): Incorrect—It attributes growing mother-daughter difference to changes in maternal habitats, but daughters settle nearby and the study does not identify such habitat change as the cause.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“female dietary mix is best understood as changeable and contingent on fluctuating environmental conditions rather than as the result of social learning or genetic factors.”): Incorrect—It excludes social learning even though the early mother-daughter match supports it, and its sweeping environmental conclusion is stronger than the modest habitat correlation.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“dietary mix among females may reflect a social learning effect that eventually diminishes, though environmental constraints cannot be ruled out as a contributing factor.”): Correct—This preserves both supported components: a maternal social-learning effect that fades and a possible environmental contribution.

questions.passage: The hwamei and other fruit-eating bird species introduced to the Hawaiian island of Oahu in the last 150 years have recently been found to spread seeds from the fruits of forest plants native to Oahu that are at risk of extinction, such as the lapalapa tree. Many of these vulnerable plant species rely on the activity of fruit-eating birds to help spread the plants’ seeds in the wild. All fruit-eating bird species native to Oahu have gone extinct, suggesting that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: non-native birds, such as the hwamei, will also be at risk of extinction if they lose access to lapalapa trees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: hwameis and other non-native birds play an important role that used to be filled by birds that were native to Oahu.

choices.label: C
choices.text: non-native birds, such as the hwamei, now spread more seeds from the lapalapa tree than birds native to Oahu did in the past.

choices.label: D
choices.text: populations of hwameis and other non-native birds will probably soon experience rapid growth.

explanation.short: Introduced fruit-eating birds now disperse seeds for vulnerable native plants, filling the ecological role lost when Oahu’s native fruit-eating birds disappeared.
explanation.key_evidence: All native fruit-eating birds are extinct, while introduced species spread seeds of native plants that depend on birds.
explanation.why_correct: The passage connects the two groups through a shared function across time: native birds formerly provided seed dispersal, and hwameis and other introduced birds now perform it for at-risk plants.
explanation.detailed: The passage supports a role-replacement inference, not a prediction about bird abundance or a numerical comparison of dispersal rates. The extinction fact matters because it identifies the missing ecological service.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“non-native birds, such as the hwamei, will also be at risk of extinction if they lose access to lapalapa trees.”): Incorrect—The passage says vulnerable plants rely on birds; it does not say non-native birds depend on lapalapa trees or would become endangered without them.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“hwameis and other non-native birds play an important role that used to be filled by birds that were native to Oahu.”): Correct—This correctly identifies seed dispersal as the important role transferred from extinct native birds to introduced birds.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“non-native birds, such as the hwamei, now spread more seeds from the lapalapa tree than birds native to Oahu did in the past.”): Incorrect—No past-versus-present seed counts are provided, so “more seeds” extrapolates beyond the evidence.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“populations of hwameis and other non-native birds will probably soon experience rapid growth.”): Incorrect—Nothing in the text predicts rapid population growth for the introduced birds.

questions.passage: Marie-Christine Doffey is the director of the Swiss National Library in Berne. In this role, Doffey ______ the library’s collections, which feature a large number of historical newspapers.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: having overseen

choices.label: B
choices.text: oversees

choices.label: C
choices.text: overseeing

choices.label: D
choices.text: to oversee

explanation.short: “Oversees” supplies the finite present-tense verb needed for what Doffey does in her current role.
explanation.key_evidence: The subject is singular “Doffey,” and the sentence describes her present responsibility as library director.
explanation.why_correct: After the introductory prepositional phrase, the clause still needs a predicate. The singular present verb “oversees” agrees with “Doffey” and completes the statement about her current duties.
explanation.detailed: A complete independent clause requires a finite verb after the subject. The other forms are participial or infinitive forms that would need an additional helping or main verb.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“having overseen”): Incorrect—“Having overseen” is a perfect participial phrase, not a finite predicate, so “Doffey having overseen” leaves the sentence incomplete.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“oversees”): Correct—“Oversees” agrees with the singular subject and states the ongoing action in a complete clause.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“overseeing”): Incorrect—“Overseeing” is a present participle and lacks a finite auxiliary such as “is.”
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“to oversee”): Incorrect—“To oversee” is an infinitive; after “Doffey” it cannot serve alone as the clause’s main verb.

questions.passage: The epic poem [i]Beowulf[/i] dates back to the 8th century. Originally ______ in Old English, it has since been translated into other languages.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: had been written

choices.label: B
choices.text: was written

choices.label: C
choices.text: is written

choices.label: D
choices.text: written

explanation.short: “Originally written in Old English” is a past-participial modifier of Beowulf that leads cleanly into the main clause.
explanation.key_evidence: The sentence already has the finite main verb phrase “has since been translated.”
explanation.why_correct: The opening element must be a modifier, not another independent predicate. The past participle “written” forms a reduced passive phrase describing the poem before the subject appears.
explanation.detailed: With choice D, the structure is “Originally written ..., it has since been translated ...”: the modifier logically attaches to “it,” referring to Beowulf, and the main clause retains its sole finite predicate.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“had been written”): Incorrect—“Had been written” is finite past perfect and would create a subordinate-looking opening with no conjunction before the main clause.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“was written”): Incorrect—after “Originally,” the finite verb phrase “was written” has no stated subject; it cannot serve as the opening modifier of “it.”
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“is written”): Incorrect—the finite present-tense phrase lacks a subject before the comma and cannot function as the required participial modifier; it also does not fit the poem’s completed eighth-century composition.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“written”): Correct—“Written” creates the required concise participial modifier and leaves “has since been translated” as the main verb.

questions.passage: Though it was designated as mission ______ mission was actually the seventy-first flight under NASA’s Space Shuttle Program.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: STS-69, the

choices.label: B
choices.text: STS-69, and the

choices.label: C
choices.text: STS-69 the

choices.label: D
choices.text: STS-69. The

explanation.short: A comma closes the dependent “Though” clause after the mission designation, allowing “the mission was” to begin the main clause.
explanation.key_evidence: “Though it was designated as mission STS-69” is subordinate; “the mission was actually ...” is the independent clause.
explanation.why_correct: A concessive clause introduced by “Though” must be separated from the following main clause with a comma. Choice A supplies that comma without adding an unnecessary coordinator.
explanation.detailed: The completed sentence contrasts the mission’s designation with its actual place in the program. Its grammar is dependent clause + comma + independent clause, not two coordinated clauses or two separate sentences.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“STS-69, the”): Correct—“STS-69, the” correctly ends the subordinate clause and begins the main clause with its subject.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“STS-69, and the”): Incorrect—Adding “and” is ungrammatical here because “Though” already subordinates the first clause; the structure does not call for coordinating it with the main clause.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“STS-69 the”): Incorrect—Without a comma after “STS-69,” the boundary between the introductory dependent clause and main clause is missing.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“STS-69. The”): Incorrect—A period strands “Though it was designated as mission STS-69” as a sentence fragment.

questions.passage: The grammar of the Kagulu language includes several noun cases common to most Bantu ______ the locative case, for instance, indicates that an action is occurring at, on, or near a particular noun.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: languages,

choices.label: B
choices.text: languages; such as

choices.label: C
choices.text: languages, such as

choices.label: D
choices.text: languages;

explanation.short: A semicolon correctly joins the complete statement about Bantu noun cases to the complete explanation of the locative case.
explanation.key_evidence: Both “The grammar ... includes ... languages” and “the locative case ... indicates ...” are independent clauses.
explanation.why_correct: Choice D preserves “the locative case” as the subject of “indicates” and uses a semicolon at the boundary between two independent clauses. No example-introducing phrase is needed.
explanation.detailed: Read the text on each side of the blank as a sentence: each side has its own subject and finite verb. A semicolon can link those closely related clauses; inserting “such as” would instead pull “the locative case” into an example phrase and disrupt the second clause.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“languages,”): Incorrect—A comma alone between the two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“languages; such as”): Incorrect—After the semicolon, “such as the locative case” cannot function as the independent-clause subject for “indicates.”
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“languages, such as”): Incorrect—The comma plus “such as” turns “the locative case” into part of an example phrase, leaving the following singular “indicates” without a proper standalone subject.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“languages;”): Correct—The semicolon marks the valid clause boundary and keeps “the locative case” as the subject of the second clause.

questions.passage: The radial velocity method, a means of indirect planetary discovery, has detected previously unknown exoplanets at vast distances from ______ the gas giant 24 Bootis b; at 522 light-years away, the Neptune-like planet CoRoT-7 c; and, as of 2023, over 1,000 other exoplanets that are too far away and dim to be observed directly.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Earth, at 313 light-years away,

choices.label: B
choices.text: Earth: at 313 light-years away,

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earth at 313 light-years away,

choices.label: D
choices.text: Earth at 313 light-years away:

explanation.short: A colon introduces the list, and a comma separates the first distance phrase from its planet name.
explanation.key_evidence: The first two parallel items are 'at313 light-years away, [planet]' and 'at522 light-years away, [planet].'
explanation.why_correct: B puts the colon after the complete general statement ending in Earth, while retaining the introductory-phrase comma inside the first list item.
explanation.detailed: The examples are semicolon-separated because the first two contain internal commas. In each, an at-distance phrase introduces the planet name. The comma after away therefore does not separate two exoplanets; it organizes the first item. The colon must precede that entire item, immediately after Earth.

choice_analysis.A: A comma does not adequately mark this complete introduction followed by an explanatory list.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: colon introduces the list; the comma follows the first item's distance phrase.
choice_analysis.C: It fails to mark the boundary before the examples and misattaches the distance to Earth.

questions.passage: Phillip Huber is well known for his work as a puppeteer. ______ he specializes in marionette puppetry. This style of puppetry involves controlling the puppet with strings from above.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By doing so,

choices.label: B
choices.text: Second,

choices.label: C
choices.text: In particular,

choices.label: D
choices.text: By contrast,

explanation.short: “In particular” narrows the general statement about Huber’s puppetry to his specific specialty, marionettes.
explanation.key_evidence: The first sentence names puppetry broadly; the second identifies marionette puppetry as Huber’s specialization.
explanation.why_correct: The logical movement is from a general field to a specific subfield. “In particular” signals exactly that narrowing before the third sentence explains the specialty.
explanation.detailed: No action, ordered list, or contrast links the sentences. The second sentence simply specifies the kind of puppetry for which the general statement should be understood.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“By doing so,”): Incorrect—“By doing so” requires a preceding action that produces his specialization, but the first sentence only states his reputation.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Second,”): Incorrect—“Second” implies an enumerated second point even though no first item has been presented.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“In particular,”): Correct—“In particular” appropriately introduces the more specific fact that he specializes in marionette puppetry.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“By contrast,”): Incorrect—“By contrast” signals opposition, but specialization in marionettes is consistent with being a puppeteer.

questions.passage: Portuguese researcher Isabel C.F.R. Ferreira reports that the homogentisic acid in oyster mushrooms benefits the mushroom by combating harmful molecules called free radicals. ______ Ferreira suggests that the acid can promote cellular health in humans, who also experience free radical damage.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For example,

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversely,

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rather,

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moreover,

explanation.short: “Moreover” adds a second benefit of homogentisic acid: after protecting mushrooms, it may also support human cellular health.
explanation.key_evidence: The acid combats free radicals in mushrooms; humans also experience free-radical damage.
explanation.why_correct: The second sentence extends the first claim to an additional beneficiary and effect. “Moreover” marks this additive relationship without implying reversal or replacement.
explanation.detailed: Ferreira’s two claims point in the same favorable direction: antioxidant protection benefits the mushroom, and the same acid may benefit human cells. The transition should accumulate evidence.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“For example,”): Incorrect—“For example” would present the human claim as an instance of a mushroom benefit, but it is a separate additional application.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Conversely,”): Incorrect—“Conversely” wrongly signals an opposite relationship even though both sentences describe benefits from combating free radicals.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Rather,”): Incorrect—“Rather” would correct or replace the first claim, which the second sentence does not do.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Moreover,”): Correct—“Moreover” correctly adds the proposed human benefit to the previously stated mushroom benefit.

questions.passage: In economics, milk is considered a soft commodity, while copper and crude oil are considered hard commodities. The categorical distinction between soft and hard commodities lies not in the products’ strength or durability but in their origin: the former type is grown or farmed, while the latter is mined or drilled. ______ pine lumber is as much a soft commodity as milk, despite its decidedly sturdier composition.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a notable exception to this rule,

choices.label: B
choices.text: Summarizing this principle,

choices.label: C
choices.text: By this definition,

choices.label: D
choices.text: Though it is grown from the earth,

explanation.short: “By this definition” applies the origin-based commodity rule to pine lumber, which counts as soft despite being sturdy.
explanation.key_evidence: Soft commodities are grown or farmed rather than mined or drilled; pine lumber comes from grown trees.
explanation.why_correct: The final sentence classifies a new example using the definition just established. “By this definition” signals that the conclusion follows from origin, not physical softness.
explanation.detailed: The apparent surprise—sturdy lumber being “soft”—is resolved by the preceding categorical rule. The transition must explicitly apply that rule rather than describe an exception to it.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“In a notable exception to this rule,”): Incorrect—Pine lumber follows, rather than excepts, the rule: its biological origin places it among soft commodities.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Summarizing this principle,”): Incorrect—The sentence applies the principle to an example; it does not summarize the principle itself.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“By this definition,”): Correct—“By this definition” accurately marks the inference from the stated origin criterion.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Though it is grown from the earth,”): Incorrect—“Though it is grown from the earth” treats the very fact that qualifies lumber as a soft commodity as a concession and creates the wrong logical emphasis.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

Contemporary Potawatomi cartographer Margaret Pearce: Indigenous cartography emphasizes “experienced space, or place, as opposed to the Western convention of depicting space as universal, homogenized, and devoid of human experience.” Pearce: “Indigenous cartographies are as diverse as Indigenous cultures, from Hawaiian performative cartographies to Navajo verbal maps and sand paintings.”
questions.prompt: The student wants to describe Shanawdithit’s approach and explain its significance. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shanawdithit’s maps are part of a broader tradition of Indigenous cartography that, according to Pearce, ranges from “Hawaiian performative cartographies to Navajo verbal maps and sand paintings.”

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Shanawdithit’s maps are part of a broader tradition of Indigenous cartography that, according to Pearce, ranges from “Hawaiian performative cartographies to Navajo verbal maps and sand paintings.””): Incorrect—The diversity examples situate Indigenous cartography broadly but omit Shanawdithit’s specific experience-based approach and its significance.
