questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Bernard Malamud was an acclaimed writer. His first published work of fiction was a short story. It was called “Benefit Performance.” It first appeared in [i]Threshold[/i] in 1943.
questions.prompt: The student wants to identify the title of Bernard Malamud’s first published short story. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard Malamud’s first published work of fiction appeared in 1943.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acclaimed writer Bernard Malamud’s first published work of fiction was a short story.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bernard Malamud’s first published short story was called “Benefit Performance.”

choices.label: D
choices.text: In 1943, a short story by Bernard Malamud appeared in [i]Threshold[/i].

explanation.short: Choice C directly identifies “Benefit Performance” as Malamud’s first published short story.
explanation.key_evidence: The notes name “Benefit Performance” and state that the short story was his first published fiction.
explanation.why_correct: The notes show that the requested information is the title, not merely the date, genre, or publication venue. Choice C pairs the exact title with its status as the first published short story.
explanation.detailed: Several choices report accurate surrounding facts, but rhetorical synthesis requires selecting the fact that accomplishes the stated goal. Only one choice actually supplies the story’s title.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Bernard Malamud’s first published work of fiction appeared in 1943.”): Incorrect—The 1943 date identifies when the first fiction appeared but omits its title.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Acclaimed writer Bernard Malamud’s first published work of fiction was a short story.”): Incorrect—Calling the work a short story gives its form but not its name.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Bernard Malamud’s first published short story was called “Benefit Performance.””): Correct—This supplies both the requested title and the first-publication relationship.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“In 1943, a short story by Bernard Malamud appeared in [i]Threshold[/i].”): Incorrect—Threshold and 1943 identify venue and date, but the sentence does not name the requested story title.

questions.passage: The following text is from Thomas Hardy’s 1874 novel [i]Far from the Madding Crowd[/i]. In the text, the narrator describes an open tract of land. The changes of the seasons are less [u]obtrusive[/u] on spots of this kind than amid woodland scenery. Still, to a close observer, they are just as perceptible; the difference is that their media of manifestation are less trite and familiar than such well-known ones as the bursting of the buds or the fall of the leaf.
questions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “obtrusive” most nearly mean?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expansive

choices.label: B
choices.text: Unyielding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conspicuous

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insolent

explanation.short: In context, “obtrusive” means conspicuous or readily noticeable, the quality the seasonal changes possess less strongly on open land.
explanation.key_evidence: The changes are “less obtrusive” yet “just as perceptible,” with less familiar signs than buds or falling leaves.
explanation.why_correct: The text distinguishes whether changes can be noticed from how familiar their signs are. “Conspicuous” means standing out to notice, so “less conspicuous” fits changes that remain perceptible to a close observer.
explanation.detailed: The narrator does not say the seasons are smaller or harsher; the point is that their manifestations attract less immediate notice than familiar woodland signals. The synonym must concern visibility to attention.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Expansive”): Incorrect—“Expansive” concerns extent or size, not how readily seasonal signs attract an observer’s notice.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Unyielding”): Incorrect—“Unyielding” means rigid or resistant and has no logical connection to the perceptibility of seasonal change.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Conspicuous”): Correct—“Conspicuous” means noticeable or prominent, matching the text’s contrast with changes that are still perceptible.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Insolent”): Incorrect—“Insolent” describes disrespectful behavior, an interpersonal meaning that cannot describe seasonal manifestations here.

questions.passage: The metal displayed in the structure of House in Kamiaraya by Kazuto Nishi Architects and the metal hardware in UE House by GENETO are representative aspects of a juxtaposition common in contemporary Japanese architecture: the [vocab]______[/vocab] of sleek, contemporary elements and traditional organic materials in a single design is a trend with both aesthetic and highly practical purposes.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: analysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: diffusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: designation

choices.label: D
choices.text: synthesis

explanation.short: “Synthesis” names the combination of sleek contemporary elements and traditional organic materials into one architectural design.
explanation.key_evidence: The passage explicitly places both contemporary metal and traditional organic materials “in a single design.”
explanation.why_correct: The sentence’s blank must express integration of different components into a whole. “Synthesis” has precisely that meaning and captures the described Japanese architectural trend.
explanation.detailed: The examples establish juxtaposition, but the defining phrase goes further by explaining that the unlike materials coexist within one design. A noun for combining elements, rather than examining or labeling them, is required.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“analysis”): Incorrect—“Analysis” means breaking something down for study; it does not describe assembling unlike materials into a building.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“diffusion”): Incorrect—“Diffusion” means spreading or dispersal, which would separate distribution rather than name a unified design combination.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“designation”): Incorrect—“Designation” is the act of naming or assigning a status, an unsupported action in the material comparison.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“synthesis”): Correct—“Synthesis” directly expresses the integration of contemporary and traditional elements into a coherent whole.

questions.passage: Described in treatises mainly published between 1768 and 1950 (such as May Florence Smith’s [i]Original Manual Course for Reading Vocal Music at Sight[/i]), musical stenography used quickly written squiggles and dots in an attempt to preserve, in print and in real time, the [vocab]______[/vocab] features of live performances—those that result from impromptu deviations of performers when fidelity to an established musical score is not mandated.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: extemporaneous

choices.label: B
choices.text: meticulous

choices.label: C
choices.text: inconspicuous

choices.label: D
choices.text: inevitable

explanation.short: Extemporaneous means improvised, matching the impromptu performance deviations.
explanation.key_evidence: The features result from 'impromptu deviations' when fidelity to a fixed score is not required.
explanation.why_correct: A directly expresses spontaneous creation without advance scripting, the quality explicitly defined after the dash.
explanation.detailed: The wording after the dash explains the adjective needed before features. The relevant distinction is between following an established score and introducing spontaneous variations. It says nothing about whether the performance is careful, easily noticed, or unavoidable. Improvisation can be meticulous; meticulous simply does not express its spontaneous origin.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: extemporaneous captures the stated impromptu origin of the variations.
choice_analysis.B: Meticulous describes carefulness, not spontaneity; carefulness is not established here.
choice_analysis.C: Inconspicuous concerns noticeability, not how the variations arise.
choice_analysis.D: Inevitable means unavoidable, but the text does not say such deviations must occur.

questions.passage: The striped marlin is ectothermic, or cold-blooded, and the Albacore tuna is a regional endotherm, meaning that parts of its body are typically warmer than the surrounding water. The basking shark had been classified as a full ectotherm, a position that became [vocab]______[/vocab] after researchers Haley R. Dolton and colleagues showed that the basking shark’s body temperature is consistently 1.0 to 1.5°C warmer than the water.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: unequivocal

choices.label: B
choices.text: untenable

choices.label: C
choices.text: inconsolable

choices.label: D
choices.text: unanticipated

explanation.short: Evidence that the shark stays warmer than surrounding water makes its classification as a full ectotherm untenable.
explanation.key_evidence: Researchers measured the basking shark at 1.0–1.5°C warmer than the water consistently.
explanation.why_correct: The passage indicates that a full ectotherm should track external temperature, so consistent internal warmth contradicts the classification. “Untenable” means no longer defensible in light of evidence.
explanation.detailed: The new measurements do not merely surprise researchers; they directly undermine the factual basis of the old position. The required word must describe a claim that cannot reasonably be maintained.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“unequivocal”): Incorrect—“Unequivocal” means unambiguous and would strengthen the old classification, the opposite of what the contrary temperature data do.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“untenable”): Correct—“Untenable” accurately describes a scientific position invalidated by consistent evidence of regional endothermy.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“inconsolable”): Incorrect—“Inconsolable” describes a person who cannot be comforted and cannot sensibly modify a classification.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“unanticipated”): Incorrect—“Unanticipated” means unexpected; even if the finding was surprising, the sentence evaluates the classification’s defensibility, not researchers’ expectations.

questions.passage: The Heege Manuscript (HM) is a collection of booklets of once-unbound paper sheets on which Richard Heege copied various texts at his fifteenth-century home between Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire in England. [u]Most other contemporaneous personal manuscripts like the Findern Anthology (FA) consist primarily of pieces by celebrated medieval authors like Gower and other readings favored by elites[/u], whereas the HM has a distinctive emphasis on the popular, including entertainments like parody romances, and the practical, with advice about health.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To illustrate how the discussion of the HM earlier in the text can improve historians’ understanding of the FA

choices.label: B
choices.text: To emphasize the ubiquity of hand-copied collections like the FA and the HM in medieval England

choices.label: C
choices.text: To suggest that the FA is a poor point of comparison for a collection like the HM

choices.label: D
choices.text: To provide context for the text’s suggestion that the HM is an outlier among collections of its time

explanation.short: The underlined comparison establishes what typical elite-oriented manuscripts contained, providing the baseline that makes the Heege Manuscript an outlier.
explanation.key_evidence: Most comparable manuscripts feature celebrated authors and elite readings; the HM instead emphasizes popular entertainment and practical advice.
explanation.why_correct: A text can be identified as unusual only against a norm. The underlined portion supplies that norm, and the following “whereas” clause contrasts the HM’s distinctive contents with it.
explanation.detailed: The Findern Anthology is not discussed for its own sake. It represents contemporaneous personal manuscripts generally, allowing readers to see why parody romances and health advice make the HM distinctive.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“To illustrate how the discussion of the HM earlier in the text can improve historians’ understanding of the FA”): Incorrect—The comparison does not show how HM scholarship improves historians’ understanding of the FA; the direction of explanation is toward the HM.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“To emphasize the ubiquity of hand-copied collections like the FA and the HM in medieval England”): Incorrect—It does not establish how common hand-copied collections were; “most other” describes content among comparables, not their prevalence in England.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“To suggest that the FA is a poor point of comparison for a collection like the HM”): Incorrect—The FA is useful precisely as a representative comparison, so calling it a poor comparison reverses the passage’s strategy.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“To provide context for the text’s suggestion that the HM is an outlier among collections of its time”): Correct—The elite-literary baseline supplies the context needed to label the HM’s popular and practical emphasis exceptional.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Michigan State University and the investment bank JPMorgan Chase are two of the many institutions offering training programs in entrepreneurship. But what results do such programs produce? In a study of college students in Poland, researcher Paul Jones and colleagues addressed this question and reported that participants who received entrepreneurial training showed strong intentions to become entrepreneurs.

Text 2

While studies of entrepreneurial training typically report positive results, a close look at these studies reveals widespread methodological shortcomings. This research literature is plagued by unclear hypotheses, insufficient sample sizes, a lack of control groups, and failures to establish pretraining baselines for the measured attributes of participants.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, the author of Text 2 would most like to know the answer to which question about Jones and colleagues’ study that is not addressed in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Did the participants that Jones and colleagues included in the study share any characteristics or life circumstances?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Did Jones and colleagues compare Polish college students who received the training with a group of successful entrepreneurs who did not receive the training?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Did Jones and colleagues measure any attributes of the participants in the study after they had received the training?

choices.label: D
choices.text: How many Polish college students did Jones and colleagues include in the study?

explanation.short: Text 2 would ask how many students were studied, since inadequate sample size is one of its explicit methodological concerns and Text 1 omits the number.
explanation.key_evidence: Text 2 flags “insufficient sample sizes”; Text 1 reports Polish college participants but gives no sample count.
explanation.why_correct: The author of Text 2 evaluates positive findings by testing named design weaknesses. Asking for the number of participants directly determines whether Jones’s study may suffer from the sample-size problem.
explanation.detailed: The question must both respond to Text 2’s critique and remain unanswered in Text 1. Participant count satisfies both conditions; other questions either misstate the proper control or ask about information already implied.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Did the participants that Jones and colleagues included in the study share any characteristics or life circumstances?”): Incorrect—Shared participant characteristics might matter generally, but Text 2’s listed criticisms do not identify demographic similarity as the relevant missing fact.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Did Jones and colleagues compare Polish college students who received the training with a group of successful entrepreneurs who did not receive the training?”): Incorrect—A valid control would be comparable students without training, not already successful entrepreneurs, so this does not test the cited lack-of-control-groups concern properly.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Did Jones and colleagues measure any attributes of the participants in the study after they had received the training?”): Incorrect—Text 1 already says the study reported post-training intentions, so some attribute was measured after training; the key missing baseline would be before training.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“How many Polish college students did Jones and colleagues include in the study?”): Correct—The participant total is absent from Text 1 and directly addresses Text 2’s concern about insufficient samples.

questions.passage: Ye Chen and John F. Canny found that a recommender system (RS)—an algorithm that generates personalized product suggestions for online shoppers—impacted consumer behavior and increased sales, a result that was corroborated by Dokyun Lee and Kartik Hosanagar. However, Lee and Hosanagar also determined that whereas an RS had a stronger positive effect on item views for utilitarian products (e.g., diapers) than for hedonic products (e.g., glass figurines), the RS had a stronger positive effect on likelihood of purchase for hedonic products than for utilitarian ones.
questions.prompt: Information in the text best supports which statement about recommender systems?

choices.label: A
choices.text: While recommender systems can affect consumer behavior toward suggested products, those effects are not uniform in nature and strength across product categories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: While recommender systems cause consumers to spend more time viewing utilitarian items such as diapers, recommender systems’ positive effect on purchase rates is likely limited to hedonic items such as glass figurines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By proposing the most useful options to consumers, recommender systems boost the online visibility of utilitarian items that otherwise tend to be overlooked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By directing customers toward specific product categories on a retailer’s website, recommender systems may limit the variety of items seen by online shoppers.

explanation.short: Recommender systems affect both viewing and purchasing, but the stronger effect switches across utilitarian and hedonic product categories.
explanation.key_evidence: The RS boosts views more for utilitarian goods but boosts purchase likelihood more for hedonic goods.
explanation.why_correct: Because product category changes both which behavior is most affected and the strength of that effect, the text supports the qualified generalization in choice A.
explanation.detailed: The findings resist a single uniform account of recommender influence. They show a positive effect overall while specifying different outcome patterns for diapers-like and figurine-like products.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“While recommender systems can affect consumer behavior toward suggested products, those effects are not uniform in nature and strength across product categories.”): Correct—This accurately captures variation in the nature and strength of RS effects across the two categories.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“While recommender systems cause consumers to spend more time viewing utilitarian items such as diapers, recommender systems’ positive effect on purchase rates is likely limited to hedonic items such as glass figurines.”): Incorrect—The study reports item views, not time spent viewing, and says the purchase effect is stronger for hedonic products—not limited exclusively to them.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“By proposing the most useful options to consumers, recommender systems boost the online visibility of utilitarian items that otherwise tend to be overlooked.”): Incorrect—The passage never says utilitarian products are overlooked or that usefulness is why the system raises their views.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“By directing customers toward specific product categories on a retailer’s website, recommender systems may limit the variety of items seen by online shoppers.”): Incorrect—No evidence concerns reduced variety of items seen; the measured outcomes are category-specific views and purchase likelihood.

questions.passage: Due to the Chorotega region’s accessibility, various types of forested areas were converted to cattle pasture as rising international meat prices drove a cattle ranching boom in the 1960s and 1970s. Juan Pablo Arroyo- Mora and colleagues used historical aerial photography and remote sensing data to track fragmentation metrics across different land use capability classes (categories that indicate possible uses of forest land). One such metric, edge density, can be used to indicate the regularity of forest patch sizes, with decreases in edge density suggesting a trend towards uninterrupted forest patches with more regular shapes. The team found a range of edge density levels, from lows of around 80 meters per hectare or less in the 1960s and 1970s for all classes, to a high in 1986 of approximately ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the assertion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 120 for Class VIII.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 50 for Class VIII.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 50 for Class VII.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 140 for Class VI.

explanation.short: The graph’s highest point in 1986 is approximately 140 meters per hectare for land-use Class VI.
explanation.key_evidence: At 1986, the Class VI series reaches roughly 140, above every other class plotted for that year.
explanation.why_correct: The sentence asks for the maximum across all class series at one year. Reading the highest 1986 marker identifies Class VI at about 140, which matches choice D.
explanation.detailed: Both coordinates matter: the value and class must correspond to the top 1986 point. Lower values or values assigned to Class VIII do not complete the stated range’s high endpoint.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“120 for Class VIII.”): Incorrect—Class VIII is not the 1986 maximum, and 120 falls below the top Class VI point.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“50 for Class VIII.”): Incorrect—A value of 50 is far below the asserted high and is incorrectly assigned to Class VIII for this purpose.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“50 for Class VII.”): Incorrect—Class VII at 50 is likewise not the highest 1986 observation.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“140 for Class VI.”): Correct—The Class VI line reaches the graph’s 1986 peak at approximately 140 meters per hectare.

questions.passage: Researchers used anonymized location data from the US and Côte d’Ivoire to document people’s daily patterns of mobility, using these results to test the efficacy of the researchers’ predictive computer model. In each country, unidirectional cycles among two, three, or four locations were empirically the most common pattern types; the graph shows each of these pattern types as a proportion of all pattern instances found for that country (e.g., the measured value for CI 3 in the graph, 0.12, indicates that the three-location pattern constituted 12% of all pattern instances in the Côte d’Ivoire data). The researchers ran their model twice under different assumptions, concluding that emphasizing the salience of local population density over personal preferences generally yielded the best results.
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to illustrate the researchers’ conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Under the assumption that density is more salient than preferences, the US 2 and CI 2 proportions are approximately 0.65 and 0.85, respectively, significantly higher than the values predicted under the other assumption and thus farther than those predictions from the measured values.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under the assumption that preferences are more salient than density, the two-location patterns (US 2 and CI 2) were predicted to be most frequent in the data even though neither proportion was projected to exceed 0.5, well below the proportion predicted under the other assumption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Under the assumption that preferences are more salient than density, the US 2 and CI 2 proportions were predicted to be in the range of 0.3 to 0.5, placing them farther from the measured values than were those predicted under the other assumption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Under the assumption that preferences are more salient than density, the US 2 and CI 2 proportions were predicted to be approximately 0.45 and 0.35, respectively, both below the measured values, whereas under the other assumption, the model overestimated the proportion for US 2 and overestimated that for CI 2.

explanation.short: For both two-location patterns, preference-heavy predictions lie much farther from the measured proportions than density-heavy predictions do.
explanation.key_evidence: US 2 and CI 2 are measured near 0.76 and 0.79; preference-heavy predictions are roughly 0.47 and 0.33, while density-heavy values are about 0.68 and 0.85.
explanation.why_correct: The graph described in the passage measures model quality by closeness to observed data. The 0.3–0.5 preference-based estimates have larger gaps from the two-location proportions than the density-based estimates.
explanation.detailed: Choice C makes the required error comparison rather than merely ranking predicted frequencies. Its examples show that emphasizing density reduces prediction error for the selected US and Côte d’Ivoire patterns.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Under the assumption that density is more salient than preferences, the US 2 and CI 2 proportions are approximately 0.65 and 0.85, respectively, significantly higher than the values predicted under the other assumption and thus farther than those predictions from the measured values.”): Incorrect—Although the density-heavy estimates are higher, the claim that they are farther from measured values reverses the graph: both are comparatively close.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Under the assumption that preferences are more salient than density, the two-location patterns (US 2 and CI 2) were predicted to be most frequent in the data even though neither proportion was projected to exceed 0.5, well below the proportion predicted under the other assumption.”): Incorrect—This notes that two-location patterns remain the largest predictions, but relative frequency alone does not establish which assumption better matches observations.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Under the assumption that preferences are more salient than density, the US 2 and CI 2 proportions were predicted to be in the range of 0.3 to 0.5, placing them farther from the measured values than were those predicted under the other assumption.”): Correct—The stated 0.3–0.5 range and greater distance from measurements correctly illustrate the density-heavy model’s better fit.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Under the assumption that preferences are more salient than density, the US 2 and CI 2 proportions were predicted to be approximately 0.45 and 0.35, respectively, both below the measured values, whereas under the other assumption, the model overestimated the proportion for US 2 and overestimated that for CI 2.”): Incorrect—Its final comparison is wrong: the density model underestimates US 2 and overestimates CI 2, not overestimating both.

questions.passage: Studies of the population density of cougars ([i]Puma concolor[/i]) have yielded a range of results, which may in part reflect differences in the effectiveness of the methods that researchers have used in their studies. For example, the difference between the maximum population density reported by Verónica A. Quiroga et al. and that reported by David M. Choate et al. might be artificially large if the use of ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?

choices.label: A
choices.text: helicopter surveying underestimates the density of cougars.

choices.label: B
choices.text: regular camera trapping underestimates the density of cougars.

choices.label: C
choices.text: regular camera trapping is impractical outside of Argentina.

choices.label: D
choices.text: helicopter surveying is more common in Utah than the use of regular camera trapping is.

explanation.short: Undercounting by regular camera traps could make Quiroga's low density estimate artificially low and the reported gap artificially large.
explanation.key_evidence: Quiroga: regular camera trapping, maximum1.26; Choate: helicopter surveying, maximum10.24 cougars per100square kilometers.
explanation.why_correct: If the lower1.26 estimate misses cougars, correcting it upward moves it toward10.24 and reduces the difference.
explanation.detailed: The reported gap is10.24−1.26=8.98. B identifies a bias that depresses the smaller estimate, so the true gap could be smaller. A instead says the larger helicopter estimate is itself too low; correcting that estimate upward would widen the gap. Lowering a higher estimate would narrow a gap, but that is not what A proposes.

choice_analysis.A: An underestimated10.24 would need upward correction, making the true difference larger rather than smaller.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: underestimating the lower camera-trap value makes the observed difference artificially large.
choice_analysis.C: Practicality in other countries does not establish bias in either estimate.
choice_analysis.D: The relative frequency of method use in Utah does not show which estimate is inaccurate.

questions.passage: Vegetation has two primary mechanisms by which it reduces air pollution: deposition (absorption of pollutants) and, the more effective, dispersion (dilution of pollutants by ventilation). Accordingly, establishment of green space to reduce major air pollutants such as fine particulate matter in urban areas receives considerable attention. Research by Zander S. Venter et al. comprised data from air-quality monitoring stations in Austria, the US state of Kentucky, and thousands of other global locations over a ten-year span, coupled with aerial imagery of those locations from the same period. The researchers ultimately recommended that reducing anthropogenic emissions remain the primary focus of urban air-quality improvement efforts.
questions.prompt: Which finding from the study, if true, would most directly account for the recommendation by Venter et al.?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The association between green space and fine particulate matter levels is moderately negative overall but becomes slightly negative and sometimes positive when consideration is limited to busy streets with tree cover heavy enough to hinder ventilation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is a predictable relationship between a location’s typical climate conditions and the efficacy of green spaces in that location, but anomalous local weather events have an outsized effect on deposition and dispersion of fine particulate matter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ambient levels of fine particulate matter are comparable across locations with comparable local infrastructure (e.g., typical building shape) but vary considerably depending on the predominant type of vegetation present.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The association between levels of fine particulate matter and green space is strongly negative for locations containing or in close proximity to major cities but becomes insignificant for more rural locations.

explanation.short: If heavy roadside tree cover can impede ventilation and sometimes coincide with higher particulate levels, green space is unreliable enough that cutting emissions should remain primary.
explanation.key_evidence: Dispersion is the stronger mechanism; choice A reports weak or positive pollution associations where dense tree cover hinders ventilation.
explanation.why_correct: Choice A connects the study result to the mechanism in the passage: vegetation may block the ventilation needed for effective dispersion. That limitation explains why green space cannot substitute for reducing pollution at its source.
explanation.detailed: The recommendation requires evidence that greenery’s benefits are conditional or can backfire in relevant urban settings. A moderately helpful overall association that weakens or reverses on busy, enclosed streets provides exactly that reason.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“The association between green space and fine particulate matter levels is moderately negative overall but becomes slightly negative and sometimes positive when consideration is limited to busy streets with tree cover heavy enough to hinder ventilation.”): Correct—This finding directly shows a practical urban condition in which green space loses or reverses its expected pollution benefit.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“There is a predictable relationship between a location’s typical climate conditions and the efficacy of green spaces in that location, but anomalous local weather events have an outsized effect on deposition and dispersion of fine particulate matter.”): Incorrect—Weather variability complicates prediction but does not show that emissions reduction should outrank green-space interventions overall.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Ambient levels of fine particulate matter are comparable across locations with comparable local infrastructure (e.g., typical building shape) but vary considerably depending on the predominant type of vegetation present.”): Incorrect—Strong variation by vegetation type could support choosing better vegetation; it does not directly justify prioritizing anthropogenic emissions.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“The association between levels of fine particulate matter and green space is strongly negative for locations containing or in close proximity to major cities but becomes insignificant for more rural locations.”): Incorrect—A strongly negative urban association would suggest green space works particularly well where needed, which weakens rather than explains the recommendation.

questions.passage: Southern Indiana’s Crawford County is among the most rural counties in the United States: the US Census Bureau classified it as 100% rural in 2010. Researchers often struggle to recruit residents of counties like Crawford for inclusion in studies. Melissa Valerio and colleagues tested whether an approach called snowball sampling improves recruitment. Working in two rural counties, they recruited a few people (known as “seeds”) with the characteristics desired for a proposed study and asked them to recruit additional participants from their social networks. Though the seeds were given minimal guidance, many more people they recruited had the desired characteristics for the study than would be expected by chance alone, most likely because ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the seeds’ social networks include a high proportion of people who share characteristics with the seeds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the seeds’ social networks tend to be somewhat smaller than the networks of people who do not live in rural areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the characteristics that made the seeds desirable for inclusion in the proposed study may be unknown to some members of the seeds’ social networks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: most seeds’ social networks include some people who do not know one another and who share few characteristics.

explanation.short: Snowball sampling succeeds when seeds know many people who share the very characteristics that made the seeds eligible.
explanation.key_evidence: Seeds recruited desired participants at rates well above chance despite receiving little guidance.
explanation.why_correct: The passage’s recruitment result is explained by social networks clustering similar people. If many contacts share a seed’s target characteristics, referrals naturally yield more eligible participants than random selection would.
explanation.detailed: The explanation must account for enrichment: why referrals contain the desired traits more often than chance. Network homophily provides that mechanism directly; network size or weak ties alone does not.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“the seeds’ social networks include a high proportion of people who share characteristics with the seeds.”): Correct—A high concentration of similar contacts predicts the observed above-chance yield from seeds’ networks.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“the seeds’ social networks tend to be somewhat smaller than the networks of people who do not live in rural areas.”): Incorrect—Smaller rural networks concern quantity of contacts, not the unusually high proportion with the desired characteristics.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“the characteristics that made the seeds desirable for inclusion in the proposed study may be unknown to some members of the seeds’ social networks.”): Incorrect—Whether contacts know which traits made the seed eligible does not cause those contacts themselves to possess the traits.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“most seeds’ social networks include some people who do not know one another and who share few characteristics.”): Incorrect—Disconnected contacts who share few characteristics predict a lower, not higher, concentration of eligible recruits.

questions.passage: Neuroscientist Artin Arshamian and his team sought to determine what affects a person’s perception of an odor as pleasant: is it culture, personal taste, or aspects of human anatomy? The team assessed odor preferences in ten groups of people with different modes of living (urban, agricultural, and hunter-gatherer) including the Semaq Beri people from a small community in the Malay Peninsula and urban dwellers from a large city in the United States. The team observed that across cultures, people generally rated odors about the same: phenethyl alcohol, which smells like roses, was typically rated more pleasant than diethyl disulfide, which smells like garlic. The team’s study thus undermined the idea that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: personal taste has little influence on whether odors are perceived as pleasant or unpleasant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: culture significantly influences whether a person perceives an odor as pleasant or unpleasant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: a person who perceives certain odors as pleasant will likely perceive the odors as roughly equal in pleasantness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: people agree in their perception of odors as pleasant or unpleasant regardless of where they live.

explanation.short: Similar odor rankings across ten culturally different groups undermine the claim that culture strongly determines whether smells seem pleasant.
explanation.key_evidence: Across urban, agricultural, and hunter-gatherer groups, rose-like phenethyl alcohol generally outranked garlic-like diethyl disulfide.
explanation.why_correct: The text indicates that culturally diverse groups broadly agreed on odor rankings. If culture significantly controlled pleasantness, substantial differences would be expected, so the agreement weakens that hypothesis.
explanation.detailed: The result supports cross-cultural similarity but does not settle every cause of individual variation. The conclusion should target the cultural-influence hypothesis the common ratings directly challenge.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“personal taste has little influence on whether odors are perceived as pleasant or unpleasant.”): Incorrect—The study compares cultures, not individuals’ idiosyncratic ratings, so it does not establish that personal taste has little influence.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“culture significantly influences whether a person perceives an odor as pleasant or unpleasant.”): Correct—This is the hypothesis contradicted by the observed agreement across groups with very different ways of life.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“a person who perceives certain odors as pleasant will likely perceive the odors as roughly equal in pleasantness.”): Incorrect—The finding ranks different odors differently; it does not suggest pleasant odors are all rated roughly equal.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“people agree in their perception of odors as pleasant or unpleasant regardless of where they live.”): Incorrect—This restates the observed cross-cultural agreement rather than naming an idea that the result undermines.

questions.passage: A soil’s microbial community (the microbial taxa present in their relative abundances) is known to affect plants’ cyclical processes. Lady Grant and colleagues hypothesized that microbial communities could also affect plants’ flavor chemistry, including volatiles and secondary metabolites like glucosinolates. Recognizing that soil’s organic content varies by location in the wild and could influence plants’ chemistry, Grant et al. introduced distinct microbial communities to individually potted mustard plants ([i]Brassica juncea[/i]) growing in a controlled environment, then measured the plants’ glucosinolates, like 3-methylthiopropyl and allyl (the most prominent), that create the spicy and bitter flavors in mustard. This method thus enabled the researchers to ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that differences in plants’ flavor chemistry result from differences in the level of glucosinolates regardless of the soil’s organic content.

choices.label: B
choices.text: disentangle the influence of microbial communities on soil’s organic content from their influence on glucosinolate content in the plants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: re-create the conditions of studies conducted in the wild that found links between soil microbial communities and levels of 3-methylthiopropyl in mustard plants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguish variations in glucosinolates due to differences in microbial communities from those that in a natural setting may be due to differences in soil’s organic content.

explanation.short: Controlled pots let the researchers isolate glucosinolate variation caused by microbial communities from variation that wild differences in soil organic content might cause.
explanation.key_evidence: Distinct microbial communities were introduced in a controlled environment after location-dependent organic content was identified as a confounder.
explanation.why_correct: The passage describes holding the growing environment controlled while varying microbial communities, removing the location-linked organic-content alternative. Glucosinolate differences can then be tied more specifically to microbial treatment.
explanation.detailed: The method is designed for causal separation, not to reproduce the wild. By controlling a known environmental confounder, it distinguishes microbial effects on flavor chemistry from effects that co-vary with natural soil conditions.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“demonstrate that differences in plants’ flavor chemistry result from differences in the level of glucosinolates regardless of the soil’s organic content.”): Incorrect—The experiment does not prove that all flavor differences result from glucosinolate levels regardless of organic content; it controls that possible influence for this test.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“disentangle the influence of microbial communities on soil’s organic content from their influence on glucosinolate content in the plants.”): Incorrect—Organic content is treated as an external location-based confounder, not as an outcome through which microbial communities exert an effect.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“re-create the conditions of studies conducted in the wild that found links between soil microbial communities and levels of 3-methylthiopropyl in mustard plants.”): Incorrect—A controlled potted environment deliberately differs from uncontrolled wild settings, so it does not re-create prior field conditions.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“distinguish variations in glucosinolates due to differences in microbial communities from those that in a natural setting may be due to differences in soil’s organic content.”): Correct—This accurately states the variable-separation benefit of varying microbes while controlling the environment.

questions.passage: There is a growing belief that teaching medical students about art alongside standard science and clinical coursework helps them become more observant, develop greater patient empathy, and strengthen their communication skills. But some medical program educators are skeptical, questioning if arts and humanities experiences can be clearly shown to have any worthwhile advantages for their students. Research into the effectiveness of arts programs for medical students by Neha Mukunda and her colleagues found that evidence is largely anecdotal and based on studies that were short in duration, limited to single institutions, or restricted to small numbers of students. To strengthen the evidence base in support of incorporating humanities into the coursework for medical students, then, ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: institutions may need to provide medical students with exposure to larger numbers of artworks than have been used in previous studies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: researchers must prove that scientific training alone is insufficient for developing clinical skills.

choices.label: C
choices.text: medical schools should highlight more student testimonials about how arts education benefits their clinical abilities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: larger-scale, multi-institutional research studies tracking outcomes for medical students over longer periods are needed.

explanation.short: The evidence gaps call for studies with more students, multiple institutions, and longer follow-up periods.
explanation.key_evidence: Existing evidence is anecdotal and comes from short, single-institution, small-sample studies.
explanation.why_correct: The passage states three weaknesses, and choice D answers each with a matching design improvement: larger scale addresses sample size, multiple institutions improve generalizability, and longer tracking addresses duration.
explanation.detailed: To strengthen an evidence base, researchers must improve the studies that produce the evidence. More testimonials would preserve the anecdotal problem, while unrelated claims about science curricula or artwork counts would not repair the cited limitations.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“institutions may need to provide medical students with exposure to larger numbers of artworks than have been used in previous studies.”): Incorrect—Increasing the number of artworks changes the intervention’s content but does not fix short duration, single-site design, or small student samples.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“researchers must prove that scientific training alone is insufficient for developing clinical skills.”): Incorrect—Proving science training insufficient is a different claim and is not required to test whether arts education provides measurable benefits.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“medical schools should highlight more student testimonials about how arts education benefits their clinical abilities.”): Incorrect—More testimonials would add anecdotal material, the very kind of evidence the review finds inadequate.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“larger-scale, multi-institutional research studies tracking outcomes for medical students over longer periods are needed.”): Correct—Larger, multi-site, longitudinal studies directly remedy all three methodological limitations named in the passage.

questions.passage: Mississippi resident Blanche Bruce, one of the nearly two thousand African Americans elected to public office during the decade that followed the Civil War, ______ his term as a member of the US Senate in 1875.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: to begin

choices.label: B
choices.text: having begun

choices.label: C
choices.text: beginning

choices.label: D
choices.text: began

explanation.short: “Began” is the finite simple-past verb that completes the clause about Bruce’s action in 1875.
explanation.key_evidence: The singular subject is “Blanche Bruce,” and the time marker “in 1875” locates a completed past event.
explanation.why_correct: The sentence needs a main predicate after the long appositive. “Began” agrees with the subject and gives the appropriate past tense for the dated action.
explanation.detailed: Remove the appositive and the core reads “Blanche Bruce ___ his term ... in 1875.” Only the simple-past finite form produces a complete independent clause.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“to begin”): Incorrect—“To begin” is an infinitive and cannot serve alone as the predicate of “Blanche Bruce.”
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“having begun”): Incorrect—“Having begun” is a participial phrase that would need another finite verb to complete the sentence.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“beginning”): Incorrect—“Beginning” is a present participle, leaving the clause without a finite main verb.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“began”): Correct—“Began” supplies the complete past-tense predicate required by the dated historical statement.

questions.passage: Occurring in the constellation Dorado, 168 thousand light-years from Earth, SN 1987A was a ______ explosion of a massive star, which blasts large amounts of radiation, heavy elements, and debris into space—that was first detected by Chilean astronomer Oscar Duhalde.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: supernova, the

choices.label: B
choices.text: supernova. The

choices.label: C
choices.text: supernova: the

choices.label: D
choices.text: supernova—the

explanation.short: A dash after “supernova” pairs with the later dash to enclose the inserted definition of a supernova.
explanation.key_evidence: The core is “SN 1987A was a supernova ... that was first detected”; the definition between “supernova” and “that” is parenthetical.
explanation.why_correct: The sentence already has a dash after “space” that closes an interruption, so matching punctuation must open it after “supernova.” Choice D creates a balanced dash pair around the definition.
explanation.detailed: When the insertion is removed, the restrictive relative clause “that was first detected ...” correctly modifies “supernova.” The paired dashes keep the explanatory material separate without breaking that core structure.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“supernova, the”): Incorrect—A comma opens the insertion but a dash closes it, producing mismatched enclosing punctuation.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“supernova. The”): Incorrect—A period wrongly ends the sentence before the definition and leaves the later dash unmatched.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“supernova: the”): Incorrect—A colon does not pair with the existing dash and would not correctly enclose the parenthetical definition.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“supernova—the”): Correct—The opening dash matches the closing dash and cleanly brackets “the explosion ... into space.”

questions.passage: [i]The Alfiyya of Ibn Malik[/i] is one of the hundreds of thousands of manuscripts that have survived from roughly the sixteenth century to the present ______ being passed down through private libraries in the city of Timbuktu, Mali. Many of these manuscripts can be found at the Alpha Mahamane Library.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: day by,

choices.label: B
choices.text: day; by

choices.label: C
choices.text: day by

choices.label: D
choices.text: day. By

explanation.short: No punctuation belongs between “present day” and the “by being passed down” phrase that explains how the manuscripts survived.
explanation.key_evidence: “By being passed down through private libraries” is an essential prepositional phrase modifying “have survived.”
explanation.why_correct: The sentence forms one continuous predicate: the manuscripts “have survived ... to the present day by being passed down.” Choice C preserves that grammatical connection.
explanation.detailed: The phrase after the blank is neither an independent clause nor a parenthetical aside. It supplies the means of survival and must remain attached without a comma, semicolon, or period.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“day by,”): Incorrect—The comma after “by” incorrectly separates the preposition from its gerund object “being passed down.”
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“day; by”): Incorrect—A semicolon cannot precede the dependent prepositional phrase “by being passed down,” since no independent clause follows it.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“day by”): Correct—“Day by” keeps the means phrase directly connected to “have survived.”
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“day. By”): Incorrect—A period makes “By being passed down through private libraries ...” a sentence fragment without a finite verb.

questions.passage: Taking a structuralist approach to analyzing Willa Cather’s novel [i]My Ántonia[/i] would lead a critic to focus on the linguistic conventions inherent in the novel. On the other hand, a postcolonial analysis ______ on narrative perspective and the representation of marginalized groups might yield a radically different interpretation of Cather’s novel.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: focuses

choices.label: B
choices.text: would be focusing

choices.label: C
choices.text: focusing

choices.label: D
choices.text: would focus

explanation.short: “Focusing” forms a participial phrase modifying “a postcolonial analysis,” leaving “might yield” as the sentence’s main predicate.
explanation.key_evidence: The clause already has the finite verb phrase “might yield a radically different interpretation.”
explanation.why_correct: The blank should add what the analysis attends to, not introduce a competing main verb. The participle “focusing” creates a modifier parallel in meaning to the earlier “Taking” phrase.
explanation.detailed: With choice C, the grammatical core is “a postcolonial analysis ... might yield ...,” and “focusing on narrative perspective ...” simply describes that analysis. Finite alternatives give the same subject two uncoordinated predicates.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“focuses”): Incorrect—“Focuses” is finite, so it clashes with the later finite predicate “might yield” without a coordinator or relative pronoun.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“would be focusing”): Incorrect—“Would be focusing” is another finite verb phrase and creates the same double-predicate problem before “might yield.”
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“focusing”): Correct—“Focusing” correctly makes the material between “analysis” and “might yield” a participial modifier.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“would focus”): Incorrect—“Would focus” supplies an unnecessary finite predicate that cannot be followed directly by the separate predicate “might yield.”

questions.passage: The neurotechnology company Kernel is working on an exciting new technology: headsets that analyze the brain’s blood flow and electrical patterns to map cortical activity. Kernel’s technology, alongside other such brain-computer interfaces that function by interpreting and executing brain signals, ______ the way for future advancements in neurotechnology.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: is paving

choices.label: B
choices.text: are paving

choices.label: C
choices.text: have paved

choices.label: D
choices.text: paving

explanation.short: The head subject “Kernel’s technology” is singular, so the predicate must be “is paving.”
explanation.key_evidence: The comma-set phrase beginning “alongside” is supplementary; its plural noun “interfaces” does not control agreement.
explanation.why_correct: Subject-verb agreement follows the head of the subject phrase, “technology.” The singular present-progressive “is paving” agrees and supplies a complete predicate.
explanation.detailed: Temporarily remove the alongside phrase: “Kernel’s technology is paving the way” is complete. Restoring the supplementary comparison does not change the verb number.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“is paving”): Correct—“Is paving” agrees with singular “technology” and expresses the ongoing contribution described.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“are paving”): Incorrect—“Are paving” incorrectly treats the nearby plural “interfaces” inside the alongside phrase as the main subject.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“have paved”): Incorrect—“Have paved” is also plural and therefore disagrees with “technology”; it additionally shifts to a completed-result tense not signaled by the sentence.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“paving”): Incorrect—“Paving” lacks the finite auxiliary needed to form the predicate after the subject.

questions.passage: The legacy of the Spanish Empire, which once controlled portions of five continents, is evident in Spanish-speaking Mexico, one of many places that reveal their imperial history in their language. Contrast Mexico with Sardinia, which ceased to be part of the empire in ______ the latter’s connection to the empire is so attenuated that Spanish is seldom spoken there today.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1720 and

explanation.short: A colon introduces the explanation of the contrast between Mexico and Sardinia.
explanation.key_evidence: 'Contrast Mexico with Sardinia, which ceased ... in 1720' is a complete imperative; 'the latter’s connection ...' begins the explanation.
explanation.why_correct: B places a colon after the complete instruction. The following clause explains why Sardinia offers a contrast with Mexico.
explanation.detailed: First locate the two clause units. The understood subject of the first is you: '[You] contrast Mexico with Sardinia.' The which clause adds information about Sardinia and ends at 1720. The following clause has its own subject, 'the latter’s connection,' and predicate. A colon can follow a complete clause when the next unit explains it. That is exactly the relationship here.

choice_analysis.A: With no boundary after 1720, the complete imperative runs into the following independent clause.
choice_analysis.B: The colon correctly links the complete instruction to its explanatory clause.
choice_analysis.C: And alone does not provide the comma needed here to join the complete imperative and the following independent clause.
choice_analysis.D: A comma alone would join two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

questions.passage: To determine the approximate age of rock carvings excavated from an archaeological site in Northern Arabia, archaeologist Maria Guagnin and colleagues collected samples of sediments surrounding the carvings; these samples were then analyzed using a method known as optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating. ______ OSL dating indicated that the carvings were at least 3,024 years old.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By comparison,

choices.label: B
choices.text: Similarly,

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ultimately,

choices.label: D
choices.text: In addition,

explanation.short: “Ultimately” presents the minimum age as the final result of collecting sediments and applying OSL dating.
explanation.key_evidence: The first sentence describes the dating procedure; the second reports its age determination of at least 3,024 years.
explanation.why_correct: The text moves from the dating process to its outcome. “Ultimately” signals that the reported age is the endpoint reached after analysis.
explanation.detailed: The passage traces a sequence from sampling to laboratory method to result. A transition for culmination fits; comparison, similarity, or mere addition would mischaracterize the age finding’s role.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“By comparison,”): Incorrect—“By comparison” requires another age or method against which the OSL result is compared, but none appears.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Similarly,”): Incorrect—“Similarly” requires a parallel finding, whereas the sentence gives the result of the single procedure just described.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Ultimately,”): Correct—“Ultimately” correctly marks the final determination produced by the OSL process.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“In addition,”): Incorrect—“In addition” treats the age as an unrelated extra fact rather than the outcome of the dating analysis.

questions.passage: Architect Victor Gruen, the designer of New Jersey’s Cherry Hill shopping mall, conceived of the mall as an indoor version of the European town square, a communal space that encouraged visitors to stroll and linger. ______ he designed Cherry Hill Mall with long, pedestrian-friendly promenades and ample seating areas clustered around fountains and greenery.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By contrast,

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accordingly,

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regardless,

choices.label: D
choices.text: In addition,

explanation.short: “Accordingly” shows that Gruen’s promenades and seating were design consequences of his communal town-square concept.
explanation.key_evidence: The intended mall would encourage strolling and lingering; the design includes pedestrian paths and gathering areas around greenery.
explanation.why_correct: The physical features implement the goal stated in the first sentence. “Accordingly” marks that plan-to-design consequence.
explanation.detailed: Long promenades facilitate strolling, while seats, fountains, and greenery encourage visitors to linger. Those details are not merely additional; they were selected in accordance with Gruen’s conception.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“By contrast,”): Incorrect—“By contrast” wrongly opposes the design features to the town-square idea even though they realize it.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Accordingly,”): Correct—“Accordingly” accurately signals that the design followed from the stated communal-space objective.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Regardless,”): Incorrect—“Regardless” would imply Gruen ignored his concept when designing, contradicting the functional match.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“In addition,”): Incorrect—“In addition” marks simple addition and misses the causal connection between the concept and design decisions.

questions.passage: In his meta-analysis of recent studies of animal information cascades, Joseph S. McCormick presents several examples of adaptive cascades (i.e., information transfers that benefit a collective), including one that involves humpback whales. However, not all cascades are beneficial. ______ his meta-analysis cites one study that described how redshanks depleted their critical energy reserves by fleeing due to flock-mates’ false alarms.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In response,

choices.label: B
choices.text: Indeed,

choices.label: C
choices.text: Instead,

choices.label: D
choices.text: In addition,

explanation.short: “Indeed” introduces the redshank study as concrete confirmation that some information cascades are harmful.
explanation.key_evidence: False alarms caused redshanks to flee and deplete critical energy reserves.
explanation.why_correct: The redshank example in the text directly substantiates the claim “not all cascades are beneficial.” “Indeed” signals this claim-to-confirming-evidence relationship.
explanation.detailed: The paragraph first contrasts beneficial cascades with possible harmful ones and then supplies a harmful case. The transition should emphasize verification, not replacement or an unrelated addition.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“In response,”): Incorrect—“In response” would require the meta-analysis or birds to react to the preceding statement, which is not the relation between claim and example.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Indeed,”): Correct—“Indeed” appropriately emphasizes that the redshank evidence confirms the asserted exception to beneficial cascades.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Instead,”): Incorrect—“Instead” signals replacement of one alternative by another, but the example does not replace the claim; it supports it.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“In addition,”): Incorrect—“In addition” only adds information and fails to mark the redshank case as evidence validating the preceding assertion.

questions.passage: As can be seen in the case of [i]Poetry[/i], a Chicago magazine published from 1912 to the present day, some small periodicals influential in the development of the modernist movement have been explored in depth by scholars. The Florentine magazine [i]The Mask[/i] (1908–1929), ______ remains among those modernist periodicals “of interest and significance about which relatively little is known,” according to scholars Peter Brooker and Andrew Thacker.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: for instance,

choices.label: B
choices.text: though,

choices.label: C
choices.text: moreover,

choices.label: D
choices.text: likewise,

explanation.short: “Though” contrasts The Mask’s limited scholarly attention with the preceding example of Poetry being studied in depth.
explanation.key_evidence: Poetry has been explored extensively; The Mask remains significant yet relatively little known.
explanation.why_correct: The passage places the two magazines in opposing scholarly positions. The parenthetical “though” marks The Mask as an exception to the pattern exemplified by Poetry.
explanation.detailed: The contrast operates within the second sentence: despite the fact that some influential small periodicals have received deep study, The Mask has not. An additive or similarity transition would erase that distinction.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“for instance,”): Incorrect—“For instance” would make The Mask another example of a deeply explored periodical, contradicting “relatively little is known.”
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“though,”): Correct—“Though” correctly introduces the contrast between scholarly attention to Poetry and neglect of The Mask.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“moreover,”): Incorrect—“Moreover” adds a reinforcing point, but the second magazine presents an opposing case.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“likewise,”): Incorrect—“Likewise” claims similarity in scholarly treatment, directly conflicting with the contrast between explored in depth and little known.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Peppercorns were used as commodity money in medieval Europe. In a commodity money economy, specific goods act as a common unit of monetary exchange that can be used to buy and sell other goods. In a barter economy, goods are traded directly between parties without the use of money. Economists Bruce Champ and Scott Freeman: bartering requires that “the person with whom you wish to trade must not only have what you want but also want what you have. The inefficiency is apparent; a great deal of time is spent merely finding someone with whom to trade.” Champ and Freeman: when “individuals might come to accept one particular good in exchange for others even if they do not wish to consume that good...barter economies essentially become monetary economies.”
questions.prompt: The student wants to paraphrase a quotation from Champ and Freeman to explain the inefficiency of barter economies. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: According to Champ and Freeman, the inefficiencies of barter economies become apparent when goods are traded between parties without the use of money.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Champ and Freeman argue that inefficient barter economies can become monetary economies if a good becomes a unit of exchange.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In a barter economy, Champ and Freeman contend, goods are traded directly between parties without the use of money, leading to inefficiency.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The precise alignment of desires that barter economies require, Champ and Freeman contend, makes them inefficient.

explanation.short: Choice D paraphrases barter’s double coincidence of wants: each trader must have what the other wants, making partner searches inefficient.
explanation.key_evidence: Champ and Freeman say a partner must both possess the desired good and want the good being offered, which consumes time.
explanation.why_correct: The notes support “precise alignment of desires” as a condensation of the quotation’s two-way matching requirement and its causal link to inefficiency. It explains, rather than merely labels, the problem.
explanation.detailed: The task specifically asks for a paraphrase of why barter is inefficient. Definitions of barter and descriptions of how money can emerge are relevant background but omit the time-consuming matching constraint in the quotation.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“According to Champ and Freeman, the inefficiencies of barter economies become apparent when goods are traded between parties without the use of money.”): Incorrect—This restates the definition of barter and asserts inefficiency without paraphrasing the required two-sided match of wants.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Champ and Freeman argue that inefficient barter economies can become monetary economies if a good becomes a unit of exchange.”): Incorrect—This uses the separate quotation about transition to commodity money, not the quotation explaining barter’s inefficiency.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“In a barter economy, Champ and Freeman contend, goods are traded directly between parties without the use of money, leading to inefficiency.”): Incorrect—Direct exchange without money is background; saying it leads to inefficiency omits the specific search problem Champ and Freeman identify.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“The precise alignment of desires that barter economies require, Champ and Freeman contend, makes them inefficient.”): Correct—“Precise alignment of desires” accurately paraphrases the need for each party to want exactly what the other offers.

questions.passage: Vexillology is the study of flags. The flags of many countries include symbols like animals, plants, or landforms. These symbols often represent an aspect of the region’s history, culture, or landscape. The flag of San Marino includes the mountain of Monte Titano. The flag of Papua New Guinea includes a raggiana bird-of-paradise.
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses information from the given sentences to emphasize a difference between the two flags?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Countries like San Marino and Papua New Guinea use symbols on their flags; examples include landforms and animals.

choices.label: B

choices.text: San Marino includes a landform on its flag, whereas Papua New Guinea’s flag includes an animal.

explanation.short: The final choice emphasizes the requested difference by directly contrasting San Marino’s landform with Papua New Guinea’s animal.
explanation.key_evidence: Monte Titano is a mountain; the raggiana bird-of-paradise is an animal.
explanation.why_correct: The given sentences require a difference-focused synthesis that assigns unlike symbol categories to the correct flags. Choice D does so explicitly with “whereas.”
explanation.detailed: The other statements group the flags under shared facts—both use symbols or both are studied by vexillologists. Only the correct sentence establishes a flag-to-flag contrast using the specific examples.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Countries like San Marino and Papua New Guinea use symbols on their flags; examples include landforms and animals.”): Incorrect—This mentions landforms and animals generally but does not say which flag contains which category, so the difference is not emphasized.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Vexillologists study flags, like those of San Marino and Papua New Guinea.”): Incorrect—This states a similarity—both are flags studied by vexillologists—and omits their symbols.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Many countries feature symbols on their flags, such as animals, plants, or landforms, and the study of these designs is known as vexillology.”): Incorrect—This defines vexillology and lists possible symbols without comparing San Marino with Papua New Guinea.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“San Marino includes a landform on its flag, whereas Papua New Guinea’s flag includes an animal.”): Correct—It correctly pairs Monte Titano’s category with San Marino and the bird-of-paradise’s category with Papua New Guinea in a direct contrast.
